### F-241 · contradiction · core §8.1 (0.44) "The round trip after a move waits for the population": only the first after each reopen waits (now observer §3.7)

> §8.1 (0.44): "So a watch session's round trip is one round trip at any
> population only until its transport first moves."

> §8.1 (0.42, as amended in 0.44): "Its round trip is then one round trip
> at any population … until its transport moves, when it waits for the
> population (below, 0.44, F-239)".

> CHANGELOG 0.44, "Deliberately not changed": "a history pays the
> population at every round trip, where this pays it once at each
> reopen."

The two sentences of §8.1 read as if every round trip after the first move
waits for the population. The CHANGELOG says it is paid once at each
reopen. Measured on zenoh-python 1.10.1 routers, the CHANGELOG is right.
A watch session in no namespace, through a link, its subscriber without
history on `ns/zk2/*/*/@zk/instance/*`; round trips asked one after
another; the link cut and healed:

| | 2,000 tokens (3 runs) | 10,000 tokens (2 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| At its start: the first, then the next two | 41–44 ms, then 0.4–0.6 ms | 42–49 ms, then 0.8–1.6 ms |
| After the reopen: the first | 145–146 ms | 3.7–4.2 s |
| After the reopen: the next three | 0.3–0.8 ms | 0.8–1.7 ms |

So the reopen's telling is paid by the first round trip after it, and the
next is one round trip again. A reader that takes the text at its word
sizes every later round trip's wait for the population. The SHOULD itself
names the right one: "wait for the round trip after a move".

**zk2py:** waits until the first round trip after a move ends. A round
trip after one that stood is not asked until the next move.

**Wording that would remove the guess:**
- "So a watch session's round trip is one round trip at any population,
  except the first after each reopen of its transport, which waits for the
  population."
- In the bullet of 0.42: "… until its transport moves: the first round
  trip after each reopen waits for the population (below)".

**Status at core 0.45:** resolved, as proposed. §8.1 now says the round
trip is "one round trip at any population but for the first after each
reopen of its transport, which waits for the reopening's telling; once
that has been sent the next is one round trip again", and 0.42's bullet
says the same. Measured again, in step 10's runs:
- the first after the reopen took 148–154 ms beside 2,000 tokens and
  3.80–3.81 s beside 10,000;
- the next, asked at once, took 0.56–0.88 ms and 1.67–1.69 ms.

Two further cases, measured for this cold read:
- **Asked from the transport event itself,** the first still waited for
  the telling: 155–165 ms and 4.7–4.9 s, in 5 of 5 runs. No round trip
  overtook the reopening's declarations.
- **Asked once the telling was over,** it took 0.6–1.0 ms and 1.8–2.4 ms.

"Waits for the reopening's telling" holds of both. 0.42's bullet says the
first "waits for the population". That holds of a first asked while the
telling is still being sent, which is what a reader that follows the
SHOULD asks. It is not a finding.

### F-242 · minor · core §8.1 (0.44): "makes the round trip again" beside "the next that needs one takes up the one in flight" (now observer §3.7)

> §8.1 (0.44): "A reader SHOULD wait for the round trip after a move …
> One whose wait ends first reads possibly incomplete (below), as before,
> and makes the round trip again."

> §8.1 (0.44), the next bullet: "A reader SHOULD NOT ask a round trip while
> one it asked since its watch session's transport last moved is in
> flight … the next that needs one takes up the one in flight, its
> caller's wait or its own having ended."

A reader whose wait ended first still has its round trip in flight. zenoh
answers it in full, and ends it at the latest at the interests timeout
(Appendix B). Read as "asks another GET", "makes the round trip again" is
what the next bullet says not to do. Read as "takes up the one in flight",
it agrees with it. Step 10's Expected supports the second reading: "it
asked one: the three it gave up on ran on, and the fourth took it up".
But a cold reader meets the first bullet first.

**zk2py:** takes it up. Its follower's next attempt, 0.2 s later, waits on
the same flight, and asks a new round trip only once that one has ended
without standing.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** "… reads possibly incomplete
(below), as before, and before its next read takes up the round trip in
flight (below), asking another only once that one has ended without
standing."

**Status at core 0.45:** resolved, as proposed: "… and before its next
read takes up the round trip in flight (below), asking another only once
that one has ended without standing (0.45, F-242)". zk2py's barrier
already did this. `readings` gains two cases (411): a wait that ended,
then the round trip taken up and ended without standing, then a second
GET; and the order the barrier reads the fake session's links in.
Beside 10,000 tokens, step 10's stand-in follower, with every wait at 20
ms, took up its round trip 16 times and asked one.

### F-243 · gap · core §8.1 (0.44) "One round trip, and one read, at a time": a GET its own timeout ended cannot be taken up, and its router still answers it (now observer §3.7)

> §8.1 (0.44): "the next that needs one takes up the one in flight, its
> caller's wait or its own having ended."

> Appendix B (0.44): "A liveliness GET whose caller drops it, times it out
> or cancels it is answered in full all the same: the session sends its
> router nothing … The runtime ends it at `routing/interests/timeout`".

A GET whose own timeout ends is over for its caller. zenoh hands it an
error reply, `Timeout`, and its final reply, and replies after that never
reach it. So there is nothing left to take up. Its router goes on
answering it all the same. Measured on zenoh-python 1.10.1, beside 10,000
tokens in `ns`, on one client session of the router, 3 runs:
- A read whose own timeout was 0.2 s: 0 tokens, 1 error reply, 0.202 s.
- A round trip's GET asked at once after it, on the same session:
  258–266 ms. On a quiet session it took 5.7–10.3 ms.
- A full read asked at once after another 0.2 s read: 0.72–0.74 s, all
  10,000.

So "its own having ended" names a case the rule cannot be followed in.
The reader holds nothing in flight. If it asks the next read at once, the
read is beside one its router is still answering, which is what the
SHOULD is meant to prevent. The reader cannot see when the router has
finished. The text does not say which it means:
- **"Its own" is a wait of the reader's,** apart from the GET's own
  timeout. Then the text should say that the GET's own timeout does not
  end it first. That means a GET asked with an own timeout above its
  session's interests timeout, where zenoh's runtime ends it.
- **Or it is the GET's own timeout.** Then the text should say what a
  reader does once a GET's own timeout ends it. "Take it up" cannot be
  done.

**zk2py:** takes the first reading. Every GET of its follower, read or
round trip, is asked with its own timeout above its session's interests
timeout (`live.flight_timeout`). Only the caller's wait ends first, and
the flight runs to its routers' final reply or to the interests timeout.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** "… takes up the one in flight,
its caller's wait having ended. A GET's own timeout ends it for its caller
alone (Appendix B), and one so ended cannot be taken up: a reader that
takes up its GETs asks each with a timeout above its session's interests
timeout, and bounds its own wait apart." Appendix B could add the cost:
measured beside 10,000 tokens, a GET asked after one its own timeout
ended waited for it, 258–266 ms against 6–10 ms on a quiet session
(zk2py).

**Status at core 0.45:** resolved, by the first reading. §8.1 now says:
- the next takes up the one in flight, "whichever wait ended first, its
  caller's or the reader's own";
- "In flight is at the reader … A GET its own timeout ends is over for
  the reader … and cannot be taken up", with its cost;
- "A reader MAY ask each GET with its own timeout at or above its
  session's interests timeout … and bound its own wait apart".

Appendix B gains the fact. Measured again, beside 10,000 tokens:
- a read with a 0.2 s timeout ended with one error reply, `Timeout`, and
  its final reply, and nothing came after them within 6 s, in 3 of 3;
- a GET whose own timeout equalled its session's 1 s interests timeout,
  through a stalled link, was ended by zenoh's runtime at 1.001–1.002 s,
  with no error reply, in 5 of 5. So "at or above" holds.

Two points of the new text are new findings. The figure it gives is a
later read's (F-246). "zk2py does so for its round trips and reads" says
more than zk2py does (F-247).

### F-244 · gap · scenarios/presence.md §10 step 10 and Expected 10 (0.44): what a runner observes from outside the reader

> step 10: "the reader under test asks its round trip four times in a row,
> giving up on the first three at once and waiting 30 s for the fourth …
> its caller asks it for its next move from a loop that also wakes every
> 20 ms, which may drop the call in flight."

> Expected 10: "The reader's round trip stands, and it asked one: the
> three it gave up on ran on, and the fourth took it up (0.44) … It asks
> one round trip after the reopen, and never a read beside one in flight,
> however often its caller drops the call (0.44)."

Asked whether step 10's Expected and the two new SHOULDs can be observed
from outside a reader: only in part.
- **Observable from outside:**
  - what the subscriber is told, at the cut and at the reopen;
  - the round trip's times;
  - the reader's verdicts: unobservable from the cut, and a complete read
    within 30 s of the heal.
- **"It asked one", "one round trip after the reopen" and "never a read
  beside one in flight"** are counts at the reader's own sessions.
  - zenoh tells a router nothing of a GET given up on (Appendix B), so
    neither a router nor a relay on the link tells one given up on from
    one waited for. zenoh-python's routers expose no per-session count of
    liveliness GETs.
  - zk2py counted them by wrapping its reader's sessions in process, each
    GET timed from its ask to its final reply.
  - A reader run as a black box cannot be judged on them. zenctl cannot.
    The zenoh lines on its stderr (`Unknown interest`, `Didn't receive
    DeclareFinal`) are a proxy, and they appear only once GETs pile up
    past the interests timeout. Their absence shows nothing.
- **"Giving up on the first three at once"** needs a reader that offers a
  round trip a caller can ask and give up on. A tool's command line
  offers none. The step does not say that this half asks the reader's own
  interface, nor that a tool may leave it out.
- **"Its caller … may drop the call in flight"** presumes a reader whose
  reads are driven by its caller's call. zk2py's follower reads on its

  too.
- **The first SHOULD's wait** is observable only in effect: a read after
  the reopen that is ordered. A reader that waited cannot be told from
  one that retried.

**zk2py:** runs step 10's counts on its own reader through its sessions,
and its analog beside it. For zenctl it reports them NOT RUN, and checks
only that the read is complete within 30 s.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** in step 10, as step 6 says its
count is the reader's own: "… it asked one (counted at the reader's watch
session: no router can tell a GET given up on, Appendix B) … a reader
whose reads do not run on its caller's call has no call to drop, and its
own waits stand in … a tool run as a black box is judged on the read
complete within 30 s alone."

- the four round trips go "through its own interface", and "a tool run

- "a reader whose reads do not run on its caller's call has none to drop,

Expected 10 says "Every count here is the reader's own, taken at its own

### F-246 · minor · core §8.1 (0.44, 0.45): "about what a read of the population costs", and F-243's figure, are a later read's (now observer §3.7)

> §8.1 (0.44): "A reader SHOULD wait for the round trip after a move, and
> run its interests timeout, above that time at its population: about
> what a read of the population costs, every matching token sent once."

> §8.1 (0.45, F-243): "a GET asked on that session meanwhile waits behind
> it: beside 10,000 tokens, 258–266 ms after a read its own 0.2 s timeout
> ended, against 6–10 ms on a quiet session (zk2py)."

> scenarios/presence.md §10, measured (0.41): "With a 120 s interests
> timeout the same read was whole, in 22.3 s. Through a tool's session …
> the read was complete with all 10,000, and again in 2.6 s".

A session's first read of a population costs several times what its
later reads do. Measured on zenoh-python 1.10.1 routers, a release build,
beside 10,000 tokens in `ns`:
- the first full read took 3.3–4.2 s, on 11 fresh sessions;
- a later read took 0.52–0.58 s;
- a read after the session's transport reopened was a later read: 0.55 s,
  in 2 of 2;
- the round trip after a reopen took 3.7–4.9 s, about a first read's cost,
  though a read on the reopened session costs a later read's.

§10's measured paragraph gives the reference's reads of 10,000 tokens,
in a debug build, as 22.3 s on one session and 2.6 s on a tool's, without
saying which was a session's first. So "about what a read of the
population costs" names two costs 7× apart.
A reader that times its own reads while it runs times later reads. Sized
on those, its interests timeout and its wait after a move would be 7–9
times short.

F-243's figure is a later read's too. Round 69 asked its 0.2 s read on a
session that had read the population before. After a session's first
read, the next GET waits for much more of its router's answer:

| The GET asked next | after a later read (3 runs) | after the session's first read (6 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| a round trip | 266–280 ms | 2.6–3.4 s |
| a full read | 783–792 ms | 3.0–3.4 s |

The rules stand either way. A GET waits behind one its own timeout
ended, and a reader waits for the round trip after a move. Only how long
the text says those take is affected.

**zk2py:** sizes nothing on a read's cost. After a move its follower waits
until the round trip ends (`move_wait_s` None), at the latest at its
watch session's interests timeout, 120 s.

**Wording that would remove the guess:**
- "… above that time at its population: about what a session's first
  read of the population costs, every matching token sent once (zk2py,
  release, beside 10,000: 3.3–4.2 s, where a later read took 0.52–0.58 s;
  a read after a reopen is a later read)."
- "… waits behind it, for what is left of its router's answer: beside
  10,000 tokens, 266–280 ms after a read its own 0.2 s timeout ended on a
  session that had read them before, and 2.6–3.4 s after a session's
  first read (zk2py)."

**Status at core 0.46:** resolved, in substance as proposed. §8.1 now
sizes the wait after a move as "about what a session's first read of the
population costs", with zk2py's figures. F-243's figure gives both cases,

- a session's first read took 3.13–3.91 s on six fresh sessions, three of

### F-248 · minor · core §8.1 (0.46, F-246): "a reader that times its own reads as it runs sees only later reads" (now observer §3.7)

> §8.1 (0.46): "A reader SHOULD wait for the round trip after a move, and
> run its interests timeout, above that time at its population: about
> what a session's first read of the population costs, every matching
> token sent once (0.46, F-246). Beside 10,000 tokens a session's first
> read took 3.3–4.2 s and a later one 0.52–0.58 s (zk2py, release), and a
> read after a reopen is a later read. So a reader that times its own
> reads as it runs sees only later reads, and sizes this wait from them
> too short."

A reader's seed is a read of the population on its reading session. When
that session has not read the population before, which is so at every
reader's start, the seed is a session's first read. Measured on
zenoh-python 1.10.1 routers, a release build, beside 10,000 tokens in
`ns`:
- zk2py's follower, started on fresh sessions, seeded in 3.13–3.91 s, in
  3 of 3;
- the next read on its reading session took 0.47–0.49 s;
- a fresh session's first read took 3.48–3.77 s, and its next 0.49–0.50
  s, in 3 of 3.

So a reader that times its own reads sees a first read once, at its seed,
and later reads after it. The cost the SHOULD names is the one it can time.
"Only" says otherwise, and could lead a reader to drop the one measure it
has. The SHOULD itself stands. The round trips after a reopen ran to 4.54
s in the same runs, past the seeds' 3.91 s, so a wait sized from a seed
needs a margin.

**zk2py:** unchanged. It sizes nothing on a read's cost. After a move its
follower waits until the round trip ends, at the latest at its watch
session's interests timeout, 120 s.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** "So a reader that sizes this wait
from its own later reads sizes it too short. Its seed, on a session that
has not read the population before, is a session's first read (zk2py's
follower: 3.1–3.9 s, the next read 0.47–0.49 s)."

**Status at core 0.47:** resolved, as proposed. §8.1 now reads "So a
reader that sizes this wait from its own later reads sizes it too short.
Its seed, on a session that has not read the population before, is a
session's first read, and the one it can time", with round 71's figures.
It adds "The round trip after a reopen ran to 4.54 s beside those seeds'
3.91 s, so a wait sized from a seed keeps a margin". zk2py reads that as
a margin kept above the seed, since the figures in the same sentence need
one. Measured again, in §10 step 10 beside 10,000 tokens, each follower on
fresh sessions:
- the default follower seeded in 3.46 s, its next read took 0.49 s, and
  its round trip after the reopen took 3.80 s, 1.10 times its seed;
- the stand-in, its waits at 20 ms, seeded in 3.39 s, and its round trip
  after the reopen took 5.18 s, 1.53 times its seed. Its reads shared the
  link with the reopen's telling.

So the margin is real, and can be half the seed. zk2py is unchanged: it
sizes nothing on a read's cost.

### F-249 · gap · scenarios/presence.md §10 Expected 10 (0.46, F-245): "unobservable from the cut", judged on a black box's output, depends on how often that output comes

> Step 10 (0.44): "Its link is cut for 1 s, and healed."

> Expected 10 (0.46, F-245): "A tool run as a black box is judged on what
> its output shows: every address it followed unobservable from the cut,
> never down, and its read complete within 30 s of the heal."

> CHANGELOG 0.46: "zk2py measured zenctl unobservable 0.41–0.49 s after
> the cut."

A black box's output can come once a period. `zenctl watchdog` prints a
transition only when it evaluates, once every `--every`, 5 s by default
(its `--help`). Until its first output after the cut, its last word is
the one before the cut, "ok". What it shows "from the cut" is therefore
its first output after the cut, if that output comes before the reader
has recovered. Step 10's run, beside 2,000 tokens in `ns`, every session
through one link cut for 1 s:
- at `--every 0.5`, as zk2py's runner sets it, it printed unobservable
  0.46–0.50 s after the cut, before the heal, in 6 of 6 (0.45–0.48 s
  beside 10,000, in 3 of 3);
- at `--every 2` it printed unobservable 1.91 s after the cut, after the
  heal, and ok at 3.92 s, in 3 of 3;
- at `--every 5`, its default, it printed nothing after the cut, so its
  output said ok throughout, in 3 of 3.

Beside 10,000 tokens, where zenctl took about 30 s to recover, it printed
unobservable 4.97 s after the cut at `--every 5`, and 1.98 s after it at
`--every 2`. So what it shows depends on its period against the time it
takes to recover, as well as against the cut.

The same tool can therefore pass, fail or be argued either way, depending
on a period the step does not set. At 2 s, reading "from the cut" as "its
first output after the cut" passes it, and reading it as "before the heal"
fails it. At its default it fails, though nothing it printed was down. The
CHANGELOG's 0.41–0.49 s were measured at `--every 0.5`, and it does not
say so. A reader under test is judged "from the move itself and before
any read" (step 6), which a white box can show. A black box can show only
what its output samples.

**zk2py:** the runner runs zenctl watchdog at `--every 0.5`, below the cut.
It reads "from the cut" as zenctl's first transition after the cut,
printed before the heal. With `--reopen`, a note gives what zenctl prints
at 5 s and at 2 s.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** "A tool run as a black box is run
with its output's period below the cut (zk2py runs zenctl watchdog at
`--every 0.5`), and judged on what its output shows: from its first output
after the cut until a complete read after the heal, every address it
followed unobservable, never down, and its read complete within 30 s of
the heal."

**Status at core 0.47:** resolved, and firmer than proposed. Expected 10
now runs a black box "with its output's period at most half the cut
(0.47, F-249: zk2py runs `zenctl watchdog` at `--every 0.5` beside the 1 s
cut), so that it prints at least once while the link is cut". It judges
it "from its first output after the cut until a complete read after the
heal", as proposed. zk2py's runner sets `--every 0.5`, half the cut, and
its check now refuses a period above half the cut. zenctl's first
transition after the cut was unobservable 0.45–0.48 s after it, before
the heal, in 3 of 3 runs, two beside 2,000 tokens and one beside 10,000.
It was ok again 1.46–1.48 s after the heal beside 2,000, and 28.5 s after
it beside 10,000. It never fired. The text does not yet say how it judges
a tool that prints nothing while the link is cut (F-252).

### F-250 · minor · core §8.1 (0.41, 0.45): "an interests timeout above their timeout" beside "its own timeout at or above its session's interests timeout" (now observer §3.3)

> §8.1 (0.41): "A reader whose GETs may wait longer SHOULD run its session
> with an interests timeout above their timeout: its long reads can then
> be complete (measured: the same read was whole, in 22 s, under a 120 s
> interests timeout)."

> §8.1 (0.45, F-243): "A reader MAY ask each GET with its own timeout at
> or above its session's interests timeout, where zenoh's runtime ends it,
> and bound its own wait apart, so that none ends before the reader can
> take it up. zk2py's follower does so for its round trips and reads".

Read word for word, the two cannot both be followed. A reader that takes
the MAY asks each GET with its own timeout at or above the interests
timeout. The SHOULD asks for an interests timeout above that same
timeout. zk2py's follower runs its sessions at 120 s, and asks every GET
with 121 s (`live.flight_timeout`). So it is the MAY's example, and by
the letter it breaks the SHOULD.

The SHOULD was written at 0.41, before a reader's wait and its GET's own
timeout were told apart. Its reason, "its long reads can then be
complete", is about how long the reader waits. Read that way the two
agree: an interests timeout above the longest the reader waits for a
read, and, under the MAY, a GET's own timeout at or above the interests
timeout. zk2py's follower waits for a read as long as its caller sets,
1 s by default and 30 s in §10 step 10, under its 120 s interests timeout.

**zk2py:** unchanged. It reads "their timeout" as the reader's own wait.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** "A reader whose reads may wait
longer SHOULD run its session with an interests timeout above the longest
it waits for one: its long reads can then be complete (…). A reader that
asks each GET with its own timeout at or above the interests timeout
(below) bounds that wait apart."

**Status at core 0.49:** resolved, as proposed. §8.1 now reads "A reader
whose reads may wait longer SHOULD run its session with an interests
timeout above the longest it waits for one", and "A reader that asks each
GET with its own timeout at or above the interests timeout (below, 0.45)
bounds that wait apart, and meets this by it", naming zk2py's follower,
120 s and 121 s. Read cold, the SHOULD and the MAY no longer meet on one
timeout: the SHOULD is about the reader's wait, the MAY about a GET's own
timeout. zk2py is unchanged, as it already read it, and its doc comments
quote 0.49.

### F-251 · minor · core §8.1 (0.42, F-233): "3.2–3.9 s (zk2py, a release build), past the scenarios' 5 s wait and zenoh's 10 s interests timeout" (now observer §3.7)

> §8.1 (0.42): "A history there brings the population back into every
> round trip: 23 s beside 10,000 tokens (the reference, a debug build),
> 3.2–3.9 s (zk2py, a release build), past the scenarios' 5 s wait and
> zenoh's 10 s interests timeout, where the round trip does not stand
> (above)."

As written, both figures are past the scenarios' 5 s wait and the 10 s
interests timeout. Only the debug build's 23 s is. zk2py's 3.2–3.9 s is
within both, and a round trip that ends there stands. The slip is zk2py's
own. Round 66's F-233 listed both figures, then said "That is past the
scenarios' 5 s round-trip wait, and past zenoh's 10 s interests timeout",
and 0.42 took the sentence over. Later rounds read it and missed it.

Measured in this round, beside 10,000 tokens in `ns`, on zenoh-python
1.10.1 routers, a release build, beside a Rust agent's builds:
- in §10 step 4, a watch session in `ns` with history, its interests
  timeout 60 s, made its round trip in 3.51, 5.87 and 3.70 s, with every
  token heard by its end;
- in step 8, zk2py's follower handed a watch session in `ns` with history
  had its round trip stand after 3.09 s.

So in a release build the history's round trip mostly fits the scenarios'
5 s wait, and once in three went past it under load. It never went past

### F-252 · minor · scenarios/presence.md §10 Expected 10 (0.47, F-249): a black box that prints nothing while the link is cut

> Expected 10 (0.47): "A tool run as a black box is run with its output's
> period at most half the cut (0.47, F-249: zk2py runs `zenctl watchdog`

> while the link is cut, and judged on what its output shows: from its
> first output after the cut until a complete read after the heal, every

> within 30 s of the heal."

"So that it prints at least once while the link is cut" holds for a tool
whose output comes every period. `zenctl watchdog`'s does not. It
evaluates once every `--every`, and prints only a transition: in this
round's runs its output after the cut was two rows, unobservable at
0.45–0.48 s and ok after the heal. The period ensures an evaluation while
the link is cut. It ensures a row only for a tool whose state moves.

output after the cut" names no output, and nothing in the window is
judged. Its read is "complete within 30 s of the heal" only by the ok it

written, the step says neither tool fails. The purpose clause points that
way, but states no verdict.

zk2py's runner fails both. Its check asks that the first transition after
the cut go from ok to unobservable, and be printed before the heal.

implementation. It decides only a tool that does not show the move.

one after it until its first that shows a complete read after the heal,

not shown the move, and fails."

### F-255 · minor · core Appendix B (0.48): "A new reader of std's `RwLock` waits behind a waiting writer"

The fact is stated for every platform. std's documentation leaves the
lock's priority policy to the operating system: a waiting writer may or
may not block new readers. The futex implementation on Linux makes new
readers wait, which is the deadlock Appendix B describes. zk2py measured
on Linux x86_64 only. The MUST NOT stands on any platform, so nothing
moves.

**zk2py:** unchanged.

**Wording that would remove the guess:** "On Linux, where std's
`RwLock` makes a new reader wait behind a waiting writer (std leaves the
policy to the platform), a declaration, an interest or a new session from
another face between two replies deadlocks the node."

**Status at core 0.50:** resolved, as proposed. Appendix B now reads
"std leaves the `RwLock`'s priority policy to the platform; on Linux its
futex lock makes a new reader wait behind a waiting writer (0.50, F-255).
There, a declaration, an interest or a new session from another face
between two replies deadlocks the node". Wording only; zk2py is
unchanged, and still measures on Linux x86_64 alone.

### F-256 · minor · core §11.1 (0.50): the MUST NOT names neither the posture nor the flow it holds for

> §11.1 (0.50): "A generator MUST NOT allow a `query` on a key expression
> that intersects one of those keys of any node, … Under `deny`, a router
> then refuses a GET of them from any principal at its ingress …"

> §11.1 (0.50), the same bullet: "Under `allow`, the generator compiles no
> admin read, and a GET wider than every deny is in none (§11.3). This
> protects a router under `deny` alone."

**The posture.** Under `default_permission: allow`, a block permits every
query no deny includes. Read as "permit", the MUST NOT is broken by every
`allow` block either generator writes:
- measured on R1, under zk2py's `allow` block and under `zenctl acl gen
  --default-permission allow`'s, the tool's GET of
  `@/*/router/queryable/**` was admitted, heard by the recorder, and
  answered with the service principal's record;
- the reference's `allow` block denies `declare_queryable` and `reply` on
  `@/**`, and no `query` there.

Read as "write an allow rule for", the MUST NOT holds under `allow` by
construction, since no allow rule is evaluated there. The last
sub-bullet says the defence is `deny`'s alone, which points to the second
reading, but the MUST itself carries no posture. A block checker has to
pick one, and its verdict on an `allow` block turns on the pick.

**The flow.** The MUST NOT names no flow. The GET that freezes a router
is the asker's, decided at the asker's face on ingress. An egress `query`
allow on `@/**` toward a principal admits no GET by itself, yet breaks
the MUST as written. Neither generator compiles one, so no verdict moves.

**zk2py:** `block_hazards` reports `allowed_query` only for a `deny`
block's allow rules, on either flow, and `allow_posture` apart, per
policy with no deny of `query` that includes `@/**`. The generator refuses

### F-261 · gap · timing.v1 §2.5: a known member of an epoch template, and "its member tokens are gone"

> §2.5: "A member never heard is judged only when the reader knows it
> another way: a known member (§0) whose owner is present."

> §2.5, Ended: "its member tokens are gone: for a template that declares
> `epoch` (core §2.3, §8.1), a complete read shows no member token of it
> (core §8.1, 0.37)."

> `deadlines.json`: "member_gone: … a known member stays held, not waited
> for, until its next arrival"

> core §8.1: "An owner with no member yet holds no member token: one that
> publishes nothing under the template holds none."

Take a consumer whose binding binds the epoch parameter, so the member is
known (§0, core R2): `pace.v1`'s `axis/{axis}` bound to `x`.
- **Its first read comes before the owner declared `x`.** The read is
  complete and shows no member token of `x`. Read as written, the member
  has ended: held, waited for by nothing until an arrival. A silent `x` is
  never reported missed. Its member token appearing later starts nothing,
  and nothing in §2.5 makes it.
- **Its first read comes after.** The member is waited for from its
  owner's interface token, and reported missed a deadline later.

So whether a known member that is declared and never published is ever
missed depends on which came first, the reader's read or the owner's
member token. Read the other way, "gone" only once a token of it was seen,
a member the owner has not declared would be missed, which core §8.1 says
does not exist yet.

It changes a verdict. zk2py reads the text as written: any complete,
ordered read that shows no member token of a held member ends it, seen or
not (`readings` shows both orders). No scenario binds the epoch parameter,
so this was not run live. Wording that would settle it: "a known member of
a template that declares `epoch` is waited for from the instant the reader
sees a member token of it, and is gone when a complete read shows none
after one was seen".

### F-262 · ambiguity · `deadlines.json`'s description: "every known member never heard and not ended is waited for from it"

> `deadlines.json`: "owner present: from unseen or absent, the owner
> became present at that instant, and every known member never heard and
> not ended is waited for from it (if started)"

> `deadlines.json`: "owner absent: every waited-for member is no longer
> waited for (a missed one stays missed)."

> §2.5: "In between it reports nothing more of the member, however long
> the silence" and "A miss already reported stands until an arrival."

A known member never heard and reported missed is "never heard and not
ended". If its owner goes absent and is present again, the description
waits for it again from that instant, and a deadline later it is missed a
second time, with no `met` between. §2.5 forbids that. No case covers it:
#11's owner never comes back.

zk2py leaves a missed member missed (`readings`: one `missed`, then `met`
at the arrival). That is v1.md's rule, so the text decides it. A reader
written from the description alone would report the miss twice. It changes
an implementation, not the text: "every known member never heard, not
missed and not ended".

### F-263 · ambiguity · timing.v1 §2.7: "present (§0) at every instant from the window's start to its end: unconfirmed or absent at none"

> §2.7: "an interval of its monotonic clock over which it subscribes to
> the resource and follows the provider's presence (core §8.1). The
> window's start is the subscription's start."

> §2.7: "The owner present throughout: present (§0) at every instant from
> the window's start to its end: unconfirmed or absent at none."

> scenarios §6, Setup: "it subscribes to `cmd` and to `axis/*`, follows
> the owner's presence as C does, reads its descriptor, and states ε =
> 100 ms."

§0 names three states: present, absent, unconfirmed. A tool that
subscribes first, as §6's setup lists its steps, holds a fourth at the
window's start: nothing read yet, which `deadlines.json` calls `unseen`
and `conclusions.json` counts as not present for a miss.
- **The bullet's two halves then disagree.** "Present at every instant"
  is false. "Unconfirmed or absent at none" is true.
- **Its first samples have no descriptor behind them.** Until the
  descriptor's GET answers, each reads `unattributed` (§2.6 step 6).

Measured, §6 step 2 with the window opened in the setup's order: the owner
was unseen for the first 1.5–2.7 ms. `cmd`'s period read unobservable
(`owner_not_present`) and its lifespan unobservable (`unattributed`).
Expected 2 says no (`not_kept`) and no (`live`).

zk2py's `Window` follows presence and holds the descriptors first, then
subscribes, and §6 passes. It changes a verdict. Wording that would remove
the guess: §2.7's "A tool follows the provider's presence, and holds its
descriptors, before its window starts", the same order in §6's setup, and
§0 naming the state before any read.

### F-264 · contradiction · timing.v1 §5: "no when any member's answer is no; yes when every member's is yes", beside the lifespan's "Finding on: Yes"

> §5: "Over a resource, or a run: no when any member's answer is no; yes
> when every member's is yes, and there is at least one; unobservable
> otherwise. A member not asked is set aside."

> §5's table, the lifespan's row: "Did a sample of this member arrive
> expired? | At least one sample expired (`expired`). | Every sample judged
> live, at least one (`live`). | … | Yes."

The sentence fits the two questions whose finding is no. Over the
lifespan, whose finding is yes, it inverts:
- a resource with one member expired and one live reads no, "no sample

- one expired beside one unobservable reads unobservable.

It also leaves "not this profile's" unsaid, which a run over a service's
resources meets.

It changes a verdict. zk2py's `rollup` reads it by each question's
finding, and `readings` shows the literal sentence's answer beside it.
Wording that would remove it: "the finding when any member's answer is the
finding; the other answer when every member's is that one, and there is at
least one; unobservable otherwise. A member not asked, or not this
profile's, is set aside."

### F-265 · gap · core §4.1 (0.53): what a node with an HLC does with an unstamped put it routes

> core §4.1: "Routers stamp puts, where timestamping is enabled. Peers and
> clients do not stamp by default." … "A session whose HLC is enabled …
> stamps every put it is not given a timestamp for, a stream sample
> included, from its own clock (0.23)." … (0.53) "moves it to the stamp of
> each put it routes, a put it receives for its own subscriber included,
> when that stamp is later than its own clock and within its delta."

> scenarios §5, Expected 2: "Every sample arrives with no stamp:
> unobservable, `unstamped`."

> core §4.2: "An unstamped sample (0.27) … put by a session with no HLC
> through no router that stamps."

Measured on zenoh-python 1.10.1, through R2 (timestamping off): beside C,
a client whose own HLC is on received 20 of 20 samples of the unstamped
owner stamped with its own zid. 0.53's bullet says what a node does with a
stamped put it routes. It does not say that a node with an HLC stamps an
unstamped one, a put for its own subscriber included. So:
- **§5 step 2** holds only for a C whose sessions have no HLC, a client's
  default, which the scenarios do not say;
- **a reader whose session serves state** (core §4.3: it MUST enable the
  HLC) never sees `unstamped`. It reads its own zid, `foreign_stamp` (§2.6
  step 7);
- **core §4.2's unstamped sample** reaches only a reader whose own session
  has no HLC. A seeded reader with one would hold it as stamped at its
  receipt (read, not measured).

For `timing.v1` it changes a test and a reason, never a pole: both are
unobservable, and nothing is discarded. For §4.2's merge it could change
what is kept. zk2py's C opens its sessions without an HLC. Wording that
would remove it:
- §4.1: "… and stamps an unstamped put it routes, a put for its own
  subscriber included, from its own clock";
- §4.2: "through no node that stamps, the reader's own session included";
- §5's setup: "C's sessions have no HLC".

### F-266 · gap · timing.v1 scenarios §1, §4, §5: when C stops, and when the owner first publishes

> scenarios §4, Setup: "Each step runs a new instance of the owner and a
> new C … The owner publishes `cmd` every 100 ms for 2 s." Expected 1:
> "Every sample's stamp carries the owner's `meta.zid`, every sample is
> live, … C reports no deadline transition."

> §1, Expected 3: "C reports `met` once, at the first arrival of step 3,
> and nothing after."

> `deadlines.json` #12: "a heard member is judged whatever presence says:
> missed with its owner absent"

Two instants are left to the runner, and each decides a check.
- **When C stops.** A deadline after the owner's last sample, `cmd` is
  missed, owner present or gone. A C that listens past it reports `missed`
  against §1 Expected 3, §4 Expected 1, 3 and 4, and §5 Expected 1. zk2py
  closes C 200 ms after the last sample.
- **When the owner first publishes.** zenoh-python handles each
  subscriber on a thread of its own: in a probe of 200 put pairs on two
  keys, one session's put then its publisher's, the second was handled
  first 82 times. So C can handle a new instance's first sample before its first
  descriptor, though core §3.3 sends the descriptor's put before any
  token. Measured, with a put at once after the owner's start: in 3, 1
  and 3 of 20 starts over three runs (`--only first`), and 8 of 30 in a
  first probe, the descriptor came up to 3.5 ms after the first sample,
  which read `unattributed`. Before the fix, §4 step 3 failed so in one of two
  full runs. zk2py's runner now publishes once C holds the descriptor.

It changes a test, not a rule: §2.6 step 6 is right to read such a sample
`unattributed`. Wording that would remove it: "C stops a deadline or less
after the owner's last sample", and "the owner publishes once C holds its
descriptor".

### F-267 · contradiction · timing.v1 scenarios §6: "each member it holds at the end of the window", beside Expected 4's `axis/x`

> scenarios §6, Setup: "It answers §5's three questions of each member it
> holds at the end of the window."

> §6, Expected 4: "`axis/x`: its member token went with the owner, so T
> reports it `ended` at that read: deadline not asked (`ended`); period
> yes (`kept`), over its span, which ended with it."

> §2.5: "a reader holds every known member, and every member it heard that
> has not ended". §2.7: "A tool answers §5's questions of each member it
> holds over a window".

`axis/x` is not known, and it ended in step 4, so T no longer holds it at
the window's end. A tool built to the setup answers nothing of it, where
Expected 4 gives two answers. §2.7's "over a window" and
`conclusions.json`'s `ended` mean a member held at any instant of the
window. Only one that ended there can be answered `ended`.

It changes a test. zk2py answers every member held in the window. Wording:
"each member it held in the window".

**Not findings.**
- **"Naming the reasons"** (§2.2) beside `conclusions.json`'s single
  `invalid`: zk2py's answer's reason is `invalid`, and its detail names
  `period_value` and the rest.
- **`next_due_ms`, "among held members heard or waited for",** leaves a
  missed member out: the description's states are heard, missed and
  waited for, and #3's `null` shows it.
- **"Missed, then forgotten"** (the description's order at an instant):
  zk2py judges every miss, then every forgetting. No case tells that from
  per member, and no report's content depends on it.
- **§1 Expected 1, "its owner present before its first sample":** C
  handled the first sample 0.2 ms before it applied its owner's token,
  which travels on its watch session. It reported nothing either way.
- **ε's type.** "In milliseconds", and every case gives an integer.
  zk2py takes any number.
- **`lost`** is zk2py's `StallWatch` over the window (core §2.7, 0.27).
  zenoh-python's callback handlers drop nothing.
- **freshness.v1 0.4** changes two sentences and no rule. zk2py's
  `Subscriber` already ages a stream by its arrival.

### F-268 · gap · arbitration.v1 §2.8: "From a move until the round trip asked after the last move stands, a consumer MUST keep every withdrawal and declaration its watch hears"

> §2.8: "When the watch session's transport closes or opens, a **move**
> … zenoh 1.10.1 can tell its subscriber withdrawn, at the close, every
> token it was told of … The rule. From a move until the round trip asked
> after the last move stands … a consumer MUST keep every withdrawal and
> declaration its watch hears … and apply none of them."

The rule assumes the consumer knows of the move before it hears the
close's withdrawals. On zenoh-python 1.10.1 it does not. The watch's
liveliness subscriber is told the close's withdrawals 0.15–0.5 ms
**before** the session's transport events listener hears the close.
- **Measured:** at 2 of 2 such closes in a probe, and at 1 to 2 of each
  actuator's 3 closes in §7's control (`--only 7c`).
- **The first close tells nothing:** the subscriber, with no history,
  had been told of no token yet.

A consumer that begins the move at the transport event applies those
withdrawals as heard. In the control, actuators switched `withdrawn`
while safety's commands never stopped, once to the dead-man.

zk2py measured that the watch session holds no link by the time each
such withdrawal is heard (`links_held` false, every time). Its
`Actuator` begins the move at the first withdrawal heard while the watch
session holds no link, and §7 passes. No withdrawal can be heard through
a session with no link but a close's own telling. zk2py cannot tell
whether Rust's zenoh orders them the same.

It changes a verdict (§7 Expected 1) and an implementation. Wording that
would remove it:
- §2.8: "A move begins at its transport event, or at a withdrawal the
  watch hears while the watch session holds no link, whichever comes
  first";
- core §8.1 or Appendix B to state the order.

### F-269 · gap · arbitration.v1 scenarios §3, Expected 2: "at the new instance's first arrival, each switches to `lab/safety`"

> §3 step 2: "2 s later, `C_s` starts again, a new instance." Expected 2:
> "When S sees the new instance's interface token, the actuators switch
> nothing; at the new instance's first arrival, each switches to
> `lab/safety`, cause `sample`."

> §2.7: "A consumer MUST NOT re-admit a provider on a sample."

The new commander puts its first `cmd` as soon as its tokens are
declared. The actuator hears the token on its watch session and the
sample on its service's session, two sessions with no order between
them. zenoh-python also handles each subscriber on a thread of its own:
in a round 76 probe, the second of two back-to-back puts was handled first in
82 of 200.

A first sample handled before the watch hears the token is a withdrawn
provider's: counted `not_active`, as §2.7 says. The switch then comes at
the next sample, 50 ms later. Measured: in 4 of 12 actuator runs, one
sample was counted `not_active` before the token. §4 step 2 avoids
this: X's puts start 500 ms after its tokens.

It changes a test, not a rule. Wording: "at the new instance's first
arrival after its watch heard the token", or the commander starting to
put 500 ms after its tokens, as §4 step 2's X does.

### F-270 · gap · arbitration.v1 §2.5: "A consumer MUST count as arrivals only the samples §2.10 accepts", evidenced by the fixture alone

> §2.5, outcome 6: "`not_incumbent`: the required interface is governed
> (`redundancy.v1` §2.2), and `redundancy.v1` §2.10 does not accept it
> … A consumer MUST count as arrivals only the samples §2.10 accepts …
> `[F: arbitrations.json]`"

`arbitrations.json` #35 gives the outcome as an input, `incumbent:
false`. No scenario governs the required interface, so a runtime that
never follows the incumbent passes every scenario. zk2py's `Actuator`
refuses a governed required interface at start, saying so: it follows no
`redundancy.v1` incumbent. That is its limitation, not the text's.

No verdict moves. A test is missing: a scenario section whose
commanders' contract uses `redundancy.v1`, a standby among them putting
raw samples.

### F-271 · ambiguity · arbitration.v1 scenarios, conventions: the counts line has no `deleted`

> scenarios.md, "What an actuator prints": `{"counts": {"providers":
> {"lab/safety": {"delivered": 40, "not_active": 0, "expired": 0,
> "not_incumbent": 0}}, "wild": 0, "unresolved": 0, "unbound": 0}}`

> §2.5: "Counted. A consumer keeps the count of each outcome, per provider
> where the sample has one (4 to 7)", outcome 4 being `deleted`.

The line two implementations are compared on lists four of the five
per-provider outcomes. zk2py prints `deleted` too, as §2.5 asks. A
reader of the example would not. It changes a test (a comparison on the
line) and is wording: the example with `"deleted": 0`.

### F-272 · gap · arbitration.v1 §5 and scenarios §10 step 4: a role read with no consumer has no binding

> §10 step 4: "T reads a copy of `rudder.v1` whose role says
> `arbitration.policy = "freshest"`, offline, with no consumer running."
> Expected 4: "The declaration: no, `invalid`, `policy_unsupported`."

> §5, the binding's row: "None beyond the premises: the binding is the
> descriptor's."

With no consumer there is no descriptor, so no binding, and no view.
`conclusions.json` takes `bindings` and has no input for "no
descriptor". Fed an empty list, the fixture's rules answer the binding
"no, `exact`", which is untrue of a binding nobody read. They answer the
selection "unobservable, `invalid`", read first. zk2py reports the three
answers and checks the declaration's alone, as Expected 4 does.

It changes a test (a tool's other two answers there), not a verdict
Expected 4 gives. Wording: the binding "not asked, `no_descriptor`" when
the tool reads no consumer's descriptor.

**Not findings.**
- **The first close tells nothing.** A watch subscriber without history
  is never told of a token declared before it, so its first close tells
  no withdrawal. The reopen's telling then declares every token it
  matches (§2.8), and each later close tells their withdrawals: F-268's
  order is met from the second close on.
- **zk2py's owner puts `ok` on `angle` at its start,** its held value of
  a raw state (core §8.2, "State values"). S sees it before any
  command, and the runner sets it aside.
- **Core 0.54's MAY** ("Acting on a withdrawal") is what the actuator
  does. It reports no absence, and reads again.
- **The lateness margin** (50 ms) was never used: the timer fires at the
  due plus 1 ns.

**After review-bot on PR #912.** Three of the actuator's faults, none the
text's:
- its round trip after a move is now asked until one stands, or a later
  move asks its own. Before, it gave up after five, and every later event
  stayed kept. While the move's events are held, it says so;
- a half-built actuator is closed whole;
- its timer can no longer spin.

`readings` shows each of them (500). Also, a binding entry that is not
`<chunk>/<chunk>` is refused. `just py-conformance`: 3405 of 3405. The
whole scenario run, `7c` included, is unchanged: 51 of 52, the one
failure F-269's strict first arrival.

## At timing.v1 0.2, arbitration.v1 0.2 and core 0.56 (#908, #909)

Round 78 read `timing.v1` 0.2, `arbitration.v1` 0.2 and core 0.55 and
0.56 cold, on main ae9cf9b7 (PR #915, #909's BB). It ran both profiles'
scenarios live in every pairing of zk2py's runtime with the reference's.

in `/srv/dev/targets/zenkey-tier/blackbox/`, their `--help` read, their
source never). It read, as a newcomer would:
- `spec/profiles/timing/v1.md` and `scenarios.md` 0.2, whole, and the
  CHANGELOG's 0.2 entry;
- `spec/profiles/arbitration/v1.md` and `scenarios.md` 0.2, whole, and
  the CHANGELOG's 0.2 entry;
- core 0.55's and 0.56's CHANGELOG entries and the text they changed:
  §4.1's new bullet, §4.2's unstamped sample, §8.1's two new bullets under
  "A round trip stands until the watch session's transport moves",
  Appendix B's three facts and Appendix C's row;

  `timing/deadlines.json` (44, eleven new), `timing/conclusions.json` (39,
  twelve new) and `arbitration/conclusions.json` (24, five new).

**timing.v1 0.2 in zk2py.**
- **`zk2py.timing`:**
  - `Tracker` takes `epoch` (F-261). A known member of an epoch template
    is waited for from the later of the start and its first member token
    seen (`member_seen`), never from its owner's presence. `member_gone`
    ends nothing before a token of the member was seen since it last
    ended. A known member gone is waited for again from a token seen
    again.
  - `beyond_bound` is reported once, while the member stays past the
    bound (F-260).
  - `tracker_for` builds no tracker under an invalid declaration, a
    deadline below the period, a resource that is not a stream, or no
    deadline (F-259).
- **The fixtures:** `deadlines.json` 44 and `conclusions.json` 39, 175 of
  175. The roll-ups passed through round 76's `rollup` unchanged. The one
  fix was the runner's: it reads a case's `resource` in place of its
  deadline, and the `rollup` cases.
- **`zk2py.timing_live`:** the `Reader` builds its trackers by
  `tracker_for`. It hands them each member token seen, heard declared or
  withdrawn or shown by a read, before that read's ends.

**arbitration.v1 0.2 in zk2py.**
- **`zk2py.arbitration`:**
  - `conclude` takes `bindings` None, no consumer's descriptor read: after
    the premises, the selection and the binding are not asked,
    `no_descriptor` (F-272);
  - `counts_line` gives every provider known, in rank order, with its five
    counts (F-271).
- **The fixtures:** `conclusions.json` 24, 120 of 120.
- **`zk2py.arbitration_live`:**
  - The `Actuator` follows a governed required interface (F-270). A
    sample counts as an arrival only when stamped by the `meta.zid` of
    the lowest instance known holding the interface's token at its
    address, as the watch and the reads show it. At its start, after its
    watch's round trip, it reads each entry's presence once and gets each
    holder's descriptor (§2.5 outcome 6). Round 77's refusal of a governed
    interface is gone.
  - It asks the round trip after an open 100 ms after the event (core
    §8.1, 0.56).
  - It prints its instants exact to the nanosecond, as the reference's
    lines do.
  - The `Commander` puts its first sample 500 ms after its tokens (F-269).
    As a `redundancy.v1` candidate (`--standby`, over zk2py's
    `Candidate`), its writer refuses while it stands by, and each refusal
    is counted. `commander raw on` puts round the writer, through its
    session, stamped by its HLC, payload `standby <n>`.
- **`zk2py.arbitration_owner`** takes the reference owner's `commander …`
  and `arbitrate counts|reads|state` words, and answers them in its JSON,
  so that one runner drives either.
- **`steer-governed.v1.toml`** was written from §11's setup, which gives no
  listing. It loads with no finding. Its fingerprint, `sha256:26b19c8c…`,

### F-273 · gap · timing.v1 scenarios §4: an owner's clock offset with its HLC on

> scenarios.md, conventions: "**The owner** is `lab/pace` … Its session's
> HLC is on … unless a section says otherwise." "**The owner's clock.**
> Where a section offsets the owner's stamping clock from C's wall clock,
> the runner sets the owner's, as `freshness.v1`'s scenarios §4 does".

> §4 step 3: "The owner's clock runs 400 ms ahead of C's for the first
> second, and agrees with it for the second."

> v1.md §2.6: "an owner may set each sample's stamp itself, from
> `Session::new_timestamp()`, which is its HLC's when one is enabled";
> "a session moves its HLC forward to a later stamp it receives".

§4 says nothing otherwise, so its owner's HLC is on. An owner whose stamps
are its HLC's cannot run 400 ms ahead and then agree: its first stamp
ahead moves its own HLC there (core §4.1, 0.53).

Measured, the reference's owner (`owner --timing`, its HLC on, `timing
offset 400`):
- its first sample was stamped 399.5 ms ahead;
- each later one carried about the same time, aged −299, −199, −99.6 ms,
  then about 0 within 400 ms: its stamping clock stood still, held by its
  HLC.

Its `--help` gives `--no-hlc` for this: "the stamps are the session's wall
clock with its zid, so `timing offset` shifts them alone (an HLC would
follow them)". With `--no-hlc`, the first second's ages were −399.7 to
−399.4 ms. zk2py's owner stamps from its wall clock plus the offset under
its zid, its HLC on, and ran 400 ms ahead for the whole second.

No verdict moves: every sample reads `clock_disagrees` either way,
falsified at the first. A test changes: a runner that checks the offset
itself fails with an owner whose HLC is on, as zk2py's did (the first
second's ages below −300 ms). zk2py's runner starts the reference's owner
with `--no-hlc` for §4. Wording that would remove it: §4's setup "The
owner's session has no HLC, so the runner's offset moves its stamps alone
(v1.md §2.6, 'Without an HLC too')".

> v1.md §2.2: "A consumer's runtime MUST refuse to start an instance
> holding a role whose declaration is invalid, as core §8.2 step 2
> refuses: no instance token appears, and nothing of the instance is

> scenarios.md §8, Expected: "no instance token of `lab/rudder-l` appears

> `owner --help`: "It is refused at start when the declaration is invalid
> … exit 1, nothing declared." "(at its start angle holds ok, the owner's
> raw state value)"

S watches `zk2/lab/**`. At each of §8's five refusals, in both pairings
with the reference's actuator and in both runs (20 of 20), S received:
- one put on `zk2/lab/rudder-l/rudder.v1/state/angle`, payload `ok`,
  about 10 ms after the process started;
- no token.

The refusal is otherwise right: exit 1, no switch, and stderr's `not
started: … arbitration.v1 invalid: <reason>`. zk2py's actuator put

The owner example puts its raw state's held value before the arbitration
check refuses it. That breaks §2.2's MUST, which the text and the
scenario state plainly. It changes the reference, and the text needs
nothing.

### F-275 · ambiguity · timing.v1 §2.5: an owner absent, beside an epoch template's known member

> §2.5: "If its owner is absent before the miss is due, the reader waits
> for nothing until the owner is present again, and counts from then."

> §2.5: "A known member of a template that declares `epoch` … is waited
> for from the later of the subscription's start and the instant the
> reader first sees a member token of it, never from its owner's
> presence".

> `deadlines.json`: "owner absent: without epoch, every waited-for member
> is no longer waited for".

The first bullet sits under "A member never heard", which since 0.2 covers
both kinds of known member, and nothing exempts an epoch template's.
- **Read with the text:** an epoch member's wait stops at its owner's
  absence, and "counts from" its owner's presence again, which the second
  bullet forbids.
- **Read with the description:** the wait goes on, and the member ends
  only when a read shows its token gone.

They differ when a complete read shows the owner's interface token gone
while the member's token is still shown, as between the two withdrawals
of a stop, or when an owner holds its member tokens on another instance.
Take: `epoch`, `axis/x` known, start 0, `member_seen` 0, owner present 0,
owner absent 50, tick 101. The description misses it, due 100; the text
reports nothing.

No case covers it: #18 and #19 end the member before the owner goes.
zk2py follows the description, so the owner's presence plays no part on
an epoch template. It changes a verdict, only in that sequence. Wording:
"If its owner is absent before the miss is due, a member waited for from
its owner's presence waits for nothing …", or one `deadlines.json` case.

### F-276 · bug · the black boxes beside the scenarios: three things a runner must work round

Each changes a test only, and the text needs nothing.
- **The commander's raw payload.** arbitration scenarios §11 step 1: "`X`,
  `C_s2`'s own session, puts `cmd` every 50 ms raw … payload `standby
  <n>`". The reference's `commander raw on` puts `safety <n>`, its own
  `<service> <n>`, so Expected 1's "S sees no `standby` payload on any
  `angle`" cannot be read by the payload. zk2py's runner tells X's
  samples by their stamp's id, `C_s2`'s zid.
- **A member token without a sample.** timing scenarios §3 step 5: "the
  owner declares `x`'s member token … and publishes nothing on it".
  `owner --timing`'s `timing add x` declares the token and publishes at
  once: S heard the token 0.7–1.2 ms after the command and the first
  sample 2.2–2.4 ms after it. No command declares the token alone. zk2py's runner declares it from a raw session
  at the owner's address.
- **`wall_ns`.** `consume --help` gives each arrival's `"wall_ns": <ns
  since the Unix epoch>`, but an expired arrival (`delivered` false)
  prints `"wall_ns": null`.

**Not findings.**
- **"How a reader holds `meta.zid`"** (§2.6, 0.2) includes "a GET again
  when a stamp's id is none it holds". zk2py's reader gets the descriptor
  of each instance presence shows, never at an unknown stamp's id. No
  scenario tells the two apart, once the runner keeps F-266's instant.
- **§2.9's "One order, instants that never go back".** zk2py's actuator
  reads its clock under its one lock, so its instants never go back.
- **§11's `C_t`** is a candidate too: `redundancy.v1` §2.5's "An instance
  of a governed interface whose election is `claim` MUST elect". The
  reference refuses to start a commander of `steer.v1` minor 1 without
  `--standby`, as zk2py's runner learned.
- **§2.8's margin after an open** is in the MUST's paragraph, and core
  0.56 makes it a SHOULD. "So a consumer asks it a margin after the open"
  reads as the way to meet the MUST, not a second rule.
- **The lowest holder, and an id that is not one** (review-bot on PR
  #916). `redundancy.v1` §2.3: "Instance ids compare as their 16
  lowercase hexadecimal digits (core §3.3, D002), character by character,
  which is their order as unsigned 64-bit integers." Core §1.2 makes an
  instance id exactly that, so ids of different lengths never meet. A
  token whose id is anything else is no zk2 token key (core §1.1). zk2py's
  key parser refuses it, so the actuator never holds it, and its
  incumbent is the least of the valid ids in that order, with no tie and
  no order left to a set. The text leaves nothing open here.
- **A sample before its holder's `meta.zid` is held** (review-bot on PR
  #916). `redundancy.v1` §2.10: "A sample it cannot attribute,
  unstamped, or under an id that is no incumbent's `meta.zid`, it
  discards", and `arbitration.v1` §2.5's outcome 6 counts what §2.10 does
  not accept as `not_incumbent`. A sample is decided at its arrival, once
  (§2.9). So one that arrives before the holder's descriptor is held is
  `not_incumbent`, and is never judged again: no verdict moves.
  - The descriptor's put precedes the tokens (core §3.3), and §2.5 asks
    for each holder's descriptor at the start, so the window is at most
    one GET.
  - zk2py's actuator subscribes to the descriptors' puts, gets each
    holder's descriptor at its start and at each token it hears, and says
    why when a GET fails.

**After review-bot on PR #916.**
- The incumbent is the least valid instance id, ordered as above
  (`Actuator.incumbent_of`).
- The commander tells a standby's refusal by its own type,
  `zk2py.owner.StandbyRefused`. Any other failed put is counted apart
  (`failed` in its `commander sent` line, zk2py's own field) and said on
  stderr.
- §8's check of zk2py's actuator is strict again: nothing at all on its
  standard output. The reference's prints `connected <endpoint>` first,
  so its check stays no switch and no `ready` line.
- §8's "nothing put" with the reference's actuator prints XFAIL, naming
  F-274. It is still counted as failed, and listed in the summary
  (`26 passed, 10 failed (10 of them known: F-274)`). The run exits 0
  only when every failure is a known one.
- Both runners skip the `rs` pairings with a line saying so when the
  black boxes are missing, and exit 2 when an `rs` pairing was asked for

Round 79 read `timing.v1` 0.3 and `arbitration.v1` 0.3 cold, on main

again in every pairing of zk2py's parties with the reference's, and both
profiles' tool sections with both tools: zk2py's and the reference's
`zenctl timing` and `zenctl arbitration`. The reference's parties and its
tool ran as black boxes (`owner`, `consume`, `zk2` and `zenctl` in
`/srv/dev/targets/zenkey-tier/blackbox/`, their `--help` read, their source
never). It read, as a newcomer would:

  CHANGELOG's 0.3 entry;
- `spec/profiles/arbitration/v1.md` and `scenarios.md` 0.3, whole, and the
  CHANGELOG's 0.3 entry;

  (45, one new), `timing/lifespans.json` (32, two new), and the
  descriptions of `timing/conclusions.json`, `timing/periods.json` and

  implementer reads them. zk2py's two tools were written from them.

**timing.v1 0.3 in zk2py.**
- **`zk2py.timing`:**
  - `tool_known`: "A tool holds no binding, so a member is known to it
    (§0) only when its template has no parameter" (§2.7);
  - `lost_for`: "A delivery the tool lost without knowing whose it was …
    is lost for every member it holds" (§2.7);
  - `owners_held`: across a face "a reader … holds an owner's `meta.zid`
    only on its deployment's word" (§2.8). Away from a face, its
    descriptors are the word.
  - The tracker already read F-275 as 0.3 writes it.
- **The fixtures:** 178 of 178. The three new cases passed the first time
  they ran.
- **`zk2py.timing_live`:**
  - The `Window` takes no binding (round 78's took `params`).
  - Across a face, the `Window` follows no presence, reads no descriptor,
    and holds only the `meta.zid` values it is given.
  - The `Reader` can follow no presence, every owner unseen (§2.5's "A
    reader that follows no presence").
- **`zk2py.timing_tool`** (new) is zk2py's tool as a process, beside
  `zenctl timing`:
  - it takes one owner's selector, reads presence and each instance's
    descriptor, and takes the revisions they name (offline, else
    retrieved, core §8.4);
  - it runs the window over the timed streams the selector reaches, and
    writes `timing: listening` on standard error at the window's start;
  - it answers §5 per member, per resource and over the run, by each
    question's finding, in one JSON document, exit 0, 1 or 2.

**arbitration.v1 0.3 in zk2py.**
- **`zk2py.arbitration`:**
  - `view_governed`: a view "reads §2.5's outcome 6 with the required
    interface governed when every revision of it the tool holds lists
    `redundancy.v1`" (§2.14);
  - `listened_ns`: "It has listened from the instant its subscriptions to
    the role's stream are declared, the last of them" (§2.14).
- **The fixtures:** 120 of 120, unchanged.
- **`zk2py.arbitration_live`:** `ToolView` is now the `Actuator`'s runtime
  with no service and no application.
  - Round 78's view had its own watch, and none of the actuator's moves,
    reads again or governed interface. It now runs the same watch, the
    same moves kept until their round trip stands, the same read again and
    the same timer.
  - It states no ε. It reads outcome 6 when every revision held governs,
    from a read at its start, after its watch's round trip, and each
    holder's descriptor.
  - It counts listening from its last subscription. Round 78's counted from
    before its watch.
- **`zk2py.arbitration_tool`** (new) is zk2py's tool as a process, beside
  `zenctl arbitration`:
  - for a consumer, it reads presence and each instance's descriptor;
  - for each role carrying a policy, it reads the declaring contract at
    the revision listed, and every revision of the required interface:
    those held offline, and those the bound providers' descriptors name,
    retrieved;
  - then it runs the view, and answers §5;
  - with `--role` and no descriptor listing it, it reads the offline
    contracts that declare the role (F-272);
  - it labels every selection the tool's own view, and writes one JSON

**Live, every pairing.** On in-process zenoh-python 1.10.1 routers, every
listener on a free loopback port, all of it under `taskset -c 0-1`:
- `python -m zk2py.timing_interop` runs `timing.v1` §1 to §5 in four

  scenario) with both tools;

### F-273 to F-276 at 0.3

Each is resolved.
- **F-273.** timing §4's setup: "The owner's session has no HLC, so the
  runner's offset moves its stamps alone (v1.md §2.6, 'Without an HLC
  too')", and the conventions run the reference's owner with `--no-hlc`
  for §4 and §5's steps 1 and 2. zk2py's runner now runs both
  implementations' owners without an HLC in §4. Over both runs, step 3's
  first second's ages were −399.9 to −398.9 ms with either owner and its
  second's 0.1 to 0.8 ms, every sample `clock_disagrees`, in all four
  pairings.
- **F-274.** The reference's: its actuator reads the declaration before
  any writer is declared or put (arbitration CHANGELOG 0.3), and its
  `--help` says "a refused actuator puts nothing". §8's "nothing put"
  passed at every refusal, 20 of 20 with the reference's actuator in each
  run. The XFAIL is gone from the runner.
- **F-275.** timing §2.5: "a member waited for from its owner's presence
  waits for nothing until the owner is present again", and "A known member
  of a template that declares `epoch` … its owner's absence stops nothing:
  it waits on until a read shows its token gone". `deadlines.json` #45 is
  round 78's sequence, missed at 101 with the owner absent, due 100.
  zk2py's tracker already read it so and passed it unchanged. Round 78's
  reading of it is gone: the fixture holds it.
- **F-276.** Each of the three, the reference's:
  - `commander raw on` puts `standby <n>`, and §11 step 1 names it. The
    runner now checks X's payload too, and both commanders' raw puts read
    `standby 0`, `standby 1`, …;
  - `timing declare <axis>` declares the token alone. §3 step 5 now drives
    the reference's owner by it, with no raw stand-in, and both readers
    passed beside it;
  - `consume --timing` prints an expired arrival's `wall_ns`, and §4
    step 2 now checks every arrival's, both readers.

### F-277 · ambiguity · timing.v1 §5: a roll-up whose every member is not asked

> §5: "Over a resource, or a run, each question is read by its finding
> (text 0.2, F-264): the finding when any member's answer is the finding;
> the other pole when every member's answer is that pole, and there is at
> least one; unobservable otherwise. A member not asked, or not this
> profile's, is set aside."

> §5's opening: "'Not asked' (nobody put the question), 'unobservable' (it
> was put, and the window could not answer it) and 'not this profile's' …
> are different facts".

> `conclusions.json` #33: `["not_this_profiles", "not_asked"]` gives
> `unobservable`, "only members not this profile's: unobservable, every one
> set aside".

The sentence and #33 make a roll-up over members all set aside
unobservable. Over a resource whose every member is not asked, nobody put
the question, which the opening calls not asked, never unobservable.

The two tools read it apart, in every step of §6 and both of §2.8's runs:
- **zk2py's tool**, by the sentence, answers `pace.v1`'s `stream/axis/{axis}`
  lifespan unobservable: no member declares `timing.lifespan_ms`, and its
  one member, `axis/x`, is `not_asked`, `no_lifespan`.
- **`zenctl timing`** answers that row `not_asked`, `no_lifespan`.
- In §6 step 4, where `axis/x` ended (`not_asked`, `ended`), the two read
  the resource's deadline apart the same way.

Over a run it moves the verdict. `zenctl timing
'zk2/lab/pace/pace.v1/stream/axis/*' --for 3 --clock-bound 100` answers
the run's lifespan `not_asked` and exits 0. zk2py's tool, on the same
window, answers it unobservable and exits 2, "no verdict".

It changes a verdict: a run's exit, and a resource row's answer. It also
needs a test: no case has every member not asked, and #33 mixes the two
kinds set aside. zk2py follows the text, and prints the difference as
XFAIL. Wording that would settle it, either way:
- "when every member is set aside: not asked when every one is not
  asked, not this profile's when every one is, unobservable otherwise
  (#32, #33)", with a case each; or
- the sentence as it stands, with a case of members all not asked, and
  the reference's roll-up fixed to it.

### Not findings

- **`whose` on every selection.** `zenctl arbitration` labels each
  selection "the tool's own view", the one not asked (`no_descriptor`)
  and the one unobservable included. §2.14's stated reference says "in
  every medium", and §10 "says each selection is its own view". zk2py's
  tool now labels every one too, and the two agree token by token.
- **A view over revisions that disagree on governance.** In §11's control,
  both tools held minor 0 offline beside minor 1, retrieved from `C_s1`'s
  descriptor. Both read the view not governed and selected `lab/safety`
  on X's samples, while both actuators followed teleop. §2.14 allows it:
  a view "may follow a provider whose samples the consumer discards", and
  "every revision" decides governance. Holding minor 1 alone, both tools
  selected teleop, with X's samples `not_incumbent`.
- **§2.7's start across a face.** The start needs a presence read and
  every descriptor it shows, and neither crosses a face (§2.8). `zenctl
  timing` waits `--settle` (0.25 s) after its subscriptions, "a margin,
  never proof". zk2py's window starts at its subscriptions. No verdict
  moves: the deadline and the period are unobservable there, and each
  sample's lifespan is judged alone. Both tools answered alike, with and
  without `--owner-zid`.
- **A loss before a member is first held.** §2.7 counts a stall "in the
  window" for "every member it holds", and zk2py's window reads so. A
  member first heard after the stall is then read lost, and its later
  miss unobservable. That reading is conservative: it never makes a false
  finding. No stall was made live.
- **`timing every` on a paused member.** The conventions: "`timing every
  <member> <ms>` publishes a member at another interval than its period".
  The black box sets the interval and leaves a paused member paused. The
  reference's drive has `cmd` on from step 2's `timing resume cmd`, and
  zk2py's runner, which pauses between windows, resumes it. This is the
  black box's interface, read from its `--help`.

**After review-bot on PR #919.**
- **Known failures by identity.** Each runner names the checks an open
  finding is known to fail, one by one, by section and name (`KNOWN`):
  F-277's roll-up at each of §6's four steps and §2.8's two readings,
  beside each owner, in `timing_interop`, and none in
  `arbitration_scenarios`. Any other failing check fails the run. A known
  check that passes prints XPASS, so its entry is seen and removed.
  `zk2py.checks` holds the summary both runners share. The roll-up check
  is now made at every step, so a fix shows as XPASS. Before, it was made
  only when the difference appeared.
- **`ToolView` and the `Actuator` share one initialiser,**
  `Actuator._init_runtime`, which sets every attribute the runtime's
  methods read. The view passes it what a tool has: no address and no
  application, no ε.
- **zk2py's arbitration tool's exit.** A finding is the
  declaration's no, the selection's `dead_man`, or the binding's yes, whose
  only reasons in §5 are `wildcard` and `shadowed`. `unbound` is the
  selection's, informative, never a finding.
- **zk2py's timing tool** exits 2 when it held no member. The empty
  roll-up is unobservable (#32, #33), and the check is now made by itself.
- §11's step 2 waits for each actuator's deadline switch before the
  tools start, and for 2 s after the hold by the clock.

After the fixes: `just py-conformance` 3449 of 3449. `timing.v1` §6 and
§2.8 with both tools beside both owners: 40 passed, the 12 F-277 checks
XFAIL, exit 0. `arbitration.v1` §10 and §11 in the four pairings: 128 of
128.

**Counts at timing.v1 0.3, arbitration.v1 0.3 and core 0.56:** 277
entries.
- **Open: F-277,** one. It changes a verdict: a resource row's answer, and

- **Resolved:** every other entry.
  - `timing.v1` 0.3 resolved F-273 and F-275, and F-276's two `timing`

  - `arbitration.v1` 0.3 resolved F-274 and F-276's commander part, both

> §5 (0.4): "the other pole when every member's answer is that pole or set
> aside, and at least one is that pole; when every member is set aside, and
> there is at least one, **not this profile's** when every one is, else

> … unobservable otherwise: a member's answer unobservable and none the
> finding, or no member at all."

It is resolved as round 79's first wording proposed, and the reference's
roll-up now follows the model alone (CHANGELOG 0.4). zk2py's
`zk2py.timing.rollup` reads it so:

  `not_asked`, with the first not-asked member's reason, as `zenctl
  timing` prints it (`no_lifespan` for `pace.v1`'s `axis/{axis}`);
- no member at all stays `unobservable`.

The four new or moved cases (the CHANGELOG's #34 and #40 to #42; #33 and
#39 to #41 in zk2py's runner, which counts from 0) failed until then, and
pass now: `timing` 181 of 181.

zk2py's tool sets a question whose run answer is set aside apart for its
exit too: 0 when every question asked, at least one, is on its other pole,
which is `zenctl timing --help`'s "0 when every question asked is answered
on its other pole over the run". Round 79's twelve F-277 checks, at each of
§6's four steps and §2.8's two readings beside each owner, now pass, and
their `KNOWN` entries are gone. In their place each tool's resource and
run roll-ups are checked against 0.4's rule over its own member rows, at
every step: both tools follow it everywhere.
